one_sentence_story: With her clever 1960–1964 Oxford mid-sentence headphone swap, Anne Treisman proved selective attention works like a dimmer knob ('Attenuation Theory') rather than an on/off switch — turning background voices down low while still letting low-threshold VIP words like your own name or primed context break straight through.
so_what_for_you: When calling someone absorbed in deep work or a noisy emergency, always say **their first name FIRST**, pause half a beat for Treisman's low-threshold alarm to swing their full spotlight toward you, and *then* speak the crucial number or instruction.

jargon_map.analogy: dimming stage lights on background actors instead of kicking them offstage

jargon_map.plain: how much signal each word in your mental lexicon needs to pop into conscious awareness — permanently low for your own name and 'Fire!', high for random words
jargon_map.analogy: smoke detectors set to hair-trigger sensitivity vs heavy vault doors

jargon_map.plain: when shadowing listeners accidentally speak 1–2 words from the 'ignored' ear right after a meaningful sentence jumps ears
jargon_map.analogy: following a melody line even when it jumps from violin to cello

jargon_map.plain: how hearing 'peanut butter and...' temporarily lowers the threshold for 'jelly' so even an attenuated whisper triggers it
jargon_map.analogy: warming up the exact next domino in line

jargon_map.plain: leading urgent communication with the listener's name + a 0.5-second beat before giving data
jargon_map.analogy: ringing the hair-trigger doorbell before handing over the package
